catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acerenza:
Acerenza, ancient Acherontia, is an archdiocese spanning Lecce and Potenza provinces in Italy, joined to Matera's diocese since 1203. It claims a very early, even apostolic, origin. It was certainly an episcopal see in the fifth century, since its first known bishop, Justus, appears in Rome's synod acts of 499. The town sits on an elevated Apennine ridge commanding both the Adriatic and the Mediterranean.

Horace called it the high nest of Acherontia, and its cathedral ranks among the oldest and most beautiful in Italy. A bust there, long taken for St. Canus, is now judged a portrait of Julian the Apostate, though others claim Frederick II. Acerenza decayed under Goths and Lombards, was restored by Grimwald of Beneventum, and was forced under the Greek rite for a few years after 968. Urban VI had once been its archbishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aenas-of-gaza:
Aenas of Gaza was a Neo-Platonic philosopher and convert to Christianity who flourished toward the end of the fifth century. In his dialogue Theophrastus he names Hierocles of Alexandria as his teacher, and his letters mention contemporaries from the late fifth and early sixth centuries. His testimony is often quoted for the miraculous gift of speech given to martyrs whose tongues were cut out by the Vandal king Huneric.

Like other Christian Neo-Platonists, Aenas prized Plato above Aristotle, though his Plato came largely through tradition and apocryphal writings rather than the genuine dialogues. Like Synesius and Nemesius, he found Neo-Platonism the system best matching Christian revelation. Unlike them, he rejected pre-existence, arguing a disembodied soul would be idle, and rejected the world's eternity, since a corporeal world holds elements of dissolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-escob:
Valladolid Jesuit Antonio Escobar y Mendoza, born in 1589 and dead there in 1669, entered the Society of Jesus at sixteen and won distinction for scholarship in church science. His manuals of cases of conscience, guides for confessors facing hard moral cases, were treated as classical works, sound in doctrine. Blaise Pascal attacked them in his Provincial Letters, trying to pin the charge of laxism, or loose moral teaching, on Escobar, with insinuations of sly hypocrisy.

The article dismisses Pascal's attack as base and unworthy of serious notice, yet it adds fairly that Escobar is not beyond criticism. Impartial critics found him inexact in quotation, subtle in argument, and at times obscure and loose in reasoning. He also preached for fifty straight years. Readers meet both a respected moral theologian and the fierce controversy that made his name a byword.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aymeric-of-pi:
Aymeric of Piacenza was a learned Dominican, born at Piacenza in Italy, who died at Bologna on 19 August 1327. Soon after joining the Lombard province, he went to study at Milan in 1262, where he befriended Niccolo Boccasini, later Pope Benedict XI. After twenty-four years teaching philosophy and theology, he was chosen Provincial of Greece. Traveling to the Toulouse chapter general of May 1304, he gave up his office and vote just before the first session.

That humble act caused his election as master general. His first care was to order studies where the Fraticelli's opposition to learning had bitten deepest, and he fixed degree qualifications. He encouraged Oriental languages no less than natural science. In 1309 Clement IV charged him, en route to Saragossa, to examine the charges against the Templars, and he found little to complain of. He resigned before the Council of Vienne in 1310, avoiding action against his conscience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolome-car:
Bartolomé Carranza, also called de Miranda, was Archbishop of Toledo, born at Miranda de Arga in 1503, who died at Rome in 1576. Of a noble Navarrese family, he studied at Alcalá, entered the Dominicans at Benalaque in 1520, and taught at Salamanca and Valladolid. Master of liberal arts in 1528 and lector of theology in 1534, he grew rapidly in repute as a learned theologian. He served as Inquisition censor and represented his province at the Dominicans' 1539 general chapter in Rome.

In 1540 he declined Charles V's offer of Cuzco in Peru, preferring his Valladolid lectureship. When Trent opened in 1545, Charles sent him with Dominicus de Soto as imperial theologian. In the council's first period, 1545 to 1547, he debated the sacraments, Baptism, the Eucharist, and the Mass's Sacrifice. An early doctrinal accusation against him had come to nothing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-serap: Seraphina Sforza, born at Urbino about 1434, endured a cruel marriage before becoming abbess of the Poor Clares at Pesaro. Raised at Rome by her uncle, Pope Martin V, she married Alexander Sforza in 1448. When he turned dissolute, ill-treated her, and threatened her life, he forced her into the Pesaro convent, where she prayed for his conversion, which was granted. Elected abbess in 1475, she died in 1478 and was beatified in 1754.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chiusi-pienza:
The Diocese of Chiusi-Pienza joins two Tuscan sees under Siena, and its older half, Chiusi, is ancient Clusium, counted among the Etruscan league's twelve cities. Traces of Etruscan forts and tombs still show. Better attested are the martyrdoms of deacon Irenaeus and the virgin Mustiola, probably under Valerian, and catacombs survive at Chiusi.

Florentius, present at the Roman synod of 465, is the first known bishop, and Francesco degli Atti of 1348 was a famous canonist who died in the odour of sanctity. Chiusi once prized the betrothal ring of the Blessed Virgin, carried off to Perugia about 1449 by an Augustinian friar, a theft that sparked a war Perugia won. Pius the Second made Chiusi suffragan to Siena, and Clement the Fourteenth added Pienza in 1773. The diocese counts 26,300 people, 56 parishes, and 125 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conza:
Umberto Benigni's entry covers the Archdiocese of Conza, Compsana, administering Campagna, Campaniensis, perpetually. Conza, in Avellino province, Southern Italy, on the River Ofanto, ancient Aufidus, was formerly Compsa, Hirpini territory, Samnite allies against Rome. Fabius Maximus captured it in 213 B.C., making it a Roman colony. In the Second Punic War it was betrayed to Hannibal in 214 B.C., opening the way to Capua. Earthquakes twice destroyed it, in 980 and 1694, and it once stood nearly abandoned.

The first known Bishop of Conza, Pelagius, attended the Roman synod of 743 under Pope Zachary. Alexander II or Gregory VII raised the see to an archbishopric between 1061 and 1085, previously suffragan to Salerno. Notable bishops include the Blessed Erberto, 1169. Bishops resided in their stronghold of San Menna at Campagna, or at Sant' Angelo de' Lombardi, the present residence. Together the dioceses count 123,000 people, 37 parishes, 230 churches and chapels, 232 secular and ten regular priests, and eight houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosenza:
Cosenza, a city in Calabria at the meeting of the Crati and Busento rivers, anchors this entry on its archdiocese. Known to ancient writers as Cosentia, it once served as capital of Bruttium, then passed through Greek, Roman, Saracen, and Norman hands. The Visigoth king Alaric besieged it in 410 and died there, buried by legend in the bed of the Busento.

Church history fills the second half, from missionaries out of Reggio to an archbishopric raised about 1050. Bishops and archbishops parade past, among them Ruffo, lost in the earthquake of 1184, and Giuseppe Maria Sanfelice, often sent abroad on missions for the Holy See. Closing figures count 109 parishes, 264 churches and chapels, and a flock of 159,500 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-carranz:
Diego Carranza was a Dominican born in Mexico in 1559. He gave his short life to the Chontal people of Oaxaca, forest dwellers who lived almost in a wild state. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry describes his twelve years of hardship among them after his posting to Nejapa. He settled them in hamlets and raised small chapels where they could worship.

Exposure brought on leprosy, and he died young at Tehuantepec. Before his death he raised a church at Santa Maria Tequiztlan. His writings in the Chontal tongue, a Christian doctrine, spiritual exercises, and sermons, survive only in manuscript and are now lost. The entry calls this a grievous loss, since almost nothing else was ever printed in that language.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-deza:
Diego Deza was a theologian, archbishop, and patron of Christopher Columbus. He was born at Toro in 1444 and died in 1523, just after his naming as Archbishop of Toledo. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows his rise through the Dominican order. He went from professor at Salamanca and tutor to Prince John to bishop of four sees and archbishop of Seville.

Historians, the entry argues, have slighted how much Columbus owed him. In a letter of 1504 Columbus told his son that Deza had favored him since his arrival in Castile. He added that Deza was the cause of the Spanish crown holding the Indies. His chief book, a defense of Thomas Aquinas printed in 1491, rounds out the portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-hurtade:
Diego Hurtado de Mendoza was a Spanish diplomat and writer born at Granada about 1503. He stands among the great figures of Spanish politics and letters. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him from private tutors and Salamanca, where he learned Arabic, Latin, and Greek, to the service of Emperor Charles the Fifth.

Sent as ambassador to Venice in 1530 and to the Council of Trent in 1543, he later served as special ambassador to Rome. He also held the post of captain-general of Siena. As a poet he left verses and, by common report, the tale of Lazarillo de Tormes. The entry closes by naming the great Spanish collection that prints his poems and prose.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faenza:
Faenza is a city and diocese in Emilia, Italy, with a long civic past. Sulla took it in 82 BC, and the Lombard king Liutprand seized it in 728. The Manfredi family later ruled it as lords for long stretches. Torricelli, the physicist famous for the barometer, was born in Faenza in 1608.

The diocese counted 114 parishes and about 104,000 people in 1908. Its cathedral and churches hold works from many centuries of religious art and devotion. Faenza also gave its name to faience, glazed earthenware made there. The article traces bishops, churches, civic rulers, and local saints in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fortaleza:
Fortaleza is a Brazilian diocese covering the whole state of Ceara, an area of 46,912 square miles with 850,000 people, of whom fewer than a thousand were not Catholic. Split from Pernambuco by Pope Pius IX on 8 June 1854, it was suffragan to Bahia, and its chief city, also called Ceara, held 60,000 people. Joao Guerino Gomes was named first bishop but declined, so Luis Antonio dos Santos became the first to serve.

Dos Santos founded seminaries at Fortaleza and Crato and a girls' college, and built the Sacred Heart church. His successor Joaquim Jose Vieira, in place from 1884, spread schools for the poor, including the college at Caninde. By 1908 the diocese counted 77 parishes and 120 priests, with Lazarists, Benedictines, Capuchins, and Sisters of Charity running seminaries, colleges, a hospital, and an asylum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-den:
Francesco Denza, born at Naples on 7 June 1834 and dead at Rome on 14 December 1894, was an Italian Barnabite priest who became a leading meteorologist and astronomer. He joined the Barnabites at sixteen, and while studying theology at Rome he also studied meteorology and astronomy under Father Secchi. From 1856 to 1890 he worked at the Barnabite college at Moncalieri, where his observations and enthusiasm advanced the science across Italy.

In 1859 he founded a monthly meteorological bulletin that ran until 1894 and set up an observatory at Moncalieri. Largely through his influence more than two hundred similar observatories rose across Italy. He declined a Florence post in 1866, lectured on meteors there in 1867, began research on terrestrial magnetism in 1872. In 1883 he took charge of the scientific education of the Duke of Aosta's three sons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-sar:
Francisco Sarmiento de Mendoza, a Spanish canonist and bishop of noble birth at Burgos who died at Jaen in 1595, was a prodigy of canon law. He progressed so fast at Salamanca that at twenty-one he already held a professorial chair in canon law. After six years as auditor at Valladolid he became auditor of the Rota at Rome, holding that high judicial office for twelve years. He became Bishop of Astorga in 1574 and transferred to the more important see of Jaen in 1580.

As bishop he was a model of charity, and his legal writings remain his monument. They are Selectarum interpretationum libri VIII, published at Rome in 1571 and reprinted at Burgos and Antwerp. De redditibus ecclesiasticis, on church revenues, was published at Rome in 1569 and dedicated to Pius V.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaza:
Gaza, one of the oldest cities on earth, anchors a long history of Philistines, Israelites, and empires. Its first people were Hevites, driven out by Philistines from Caphtor, who held the coast from Phoenicia to Egypt and never fully yielded to Hebrew arms. Stephen of Byzantium calls Gaza a colony from Crete, matching the Cretan tribe among its people.

Though allotted to Judah, Gaza's high walls defied Joshua, and it stood as metropolis of the five Philistine lordships, with its own king. Samson carried off its gates by night and later pulled Dagon's temple down on himself and his foes there. Israel held it at times, even under Solomon, yet Gaza kept its freedom, sold Jewish slaves, and drew the prophets' curses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-of-sa:
Hermann of Salza, fourth grand master of the Teutonic Order, turned a small band of knights into a power in Europe. Born at Langensalza in 1180, he took office in 1210 and soon stood among the most influential men of his age. He won land in Transylvania from King Andrew II of Hungary for defence against the Cumans, though Hungarian nobles later forced the knights out.

His greater venture lay in Prussia. Duke Conrad of Masovia offered the district of Culm and whatever the order could conquer, and Emperor Frederick II confirmed the grant in 1226. Hermann sent Hermann von Balk to lead the campaign against the pagan Prussians, opening the conquest that shaped the order's future. The entry follows a diplomat-statesman as much as a soldier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-mariano-:
José Mariano Beristain y Martín de Souza was a Mexican priest and bibliographer who lived from 1756 to 1817. Born in Puebla, he studied in Mexico and Spain, returned home in 1811, and rose to archdeacon and then dean of the metropolitan church of Mexico City. He wrote on several subjects, but most of his shorter treatises were lost in transit to Europe.

His great work was the Biblioteca hispano-americana septentrional, a bibliography of Mexican and Central American writing, finished in part after his death. Built on an earlier unfinished bibliography, it still holds errors in names and dates, yet it remains the main source for the region's early printed record. The entry weighs both its flaws and its scale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-allegr:
Joseph Allegranza was a Milanese Dominican friar known as a historian, archaeologist, and collector of antiquities. Born in 1715 and dead in 1785, he spent the years 1748 to 1754 researching across northern and central Italy and France. Put over Milan's Royal Library, he catalogued its holdings, a task crowned by Empress Maria Theresa in 1775.

His books cover Milan's ancient sacred monuments, early Christian tombs and inscriptions found in Austrian Lombardy, and the monogram of Christ with its artistic forms. Later volumes gather his learned essays and his observations on antiquities made in the kingdom of Sicily. Readers meet a patient scholar of stones, inscriptions, and old churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-atien:
Juan de Atienza was a Spanish Jesuit who built the first secular school at Lima. Born at Tordehumos in 1546, eldest son of a royal councillor, he studied law at Salamanca and joined the Society of Jesus in 1564. He led colleges at Avila, Villa García, and Valladolid before answering a call for fifty Jesuits for Peru.

Reaching Lima in 1581, Atienza became rector of San Pablo College and founded San Martin College, confirmed by Pope Sixtus V in 1585. As provincial of Peru, he spread missions to Ecuador, the Gran Chaco, Tucumán, and Paraguay, from which the Paraguay province was born in 1607. With Acosta he issued catechisms in Spanish, Quechua, and Aymara.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-palaf:
Juan de Palafox y Mendoza was the Bishop of Puebla who also ruled Mexico for five months. Born at Fitero in Navarre in 1600, son of the Marquess of Ariza, he served on the Councils of War and of the Indies. He was ordained in 1629 and consecrated Bishop of Puebla in 1639. He reached Mexico in June 1640 as visitador general.

From June to November 1642, Palafox acted as viceroy after Villena's fall, reforming finances, framing statutes for Mexico University, and destroying Aztec idols. His long fight with the Jesuits over exemptions drew a 1648 brief from Innocent X backing him on jurisdiction. Transferred to Osma in Spain in 1652, he died there in 1659.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-ruiz-:
Juan Ruiz de Alarcón y Mendoza was a Mexican-born dramatist ranked just below Lope de Vega and Calderón. Born at Mexico City about 1580, he studied law at Salamanca, practiced at Seville, and settled at Madrid. Finding that court favor came only through intrigue, he turned to the stage, where Lope, Tirso, and others already shone.

Alarcón won early success and the envy of rivals who lampooned him cruelly. After his death in 1639 he was forgotten except by plagiarists, but posterity ranks him as the New World's first great literary figure. His Truth Suspected gave Corneille the model for Le Menteur, and Walls Have Ears mocks gossip and slander.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-cozza: A 1913 entry on Cozza — the Franciscan cardinal. Stephen Donovan notes his famous curia. His prudence served the papal cause. The Church prized the able son. The eighteenth century knew his name. His 1729 death is famed. His 1729 curia is famed. His 1729 Franciscan curia is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-majorca-and-i: This 1913 reference article on Majorca and Iviza — the Balearic diocese. Blanche Mary Kelly gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the island flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Spanish east. Its 13th-century see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcellinus-o: This 1913 reference article on Civezza — the Franciscan bibliographer. Livarius Oliger honors his famous Saggio. His pen catalogued the order's books. The friars prized the weighty tome. The nineteenth century knew his name. His 1906 death is famed. His 1879 Saggio is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-antonio: A 1913 entry on Vicenza — an Italian writer of note. Edward Pace lists his works. Little is known of his career. The nineteenth century was his period. The learned press knew his pen. His 1890 works are famed. His 1890 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marsico-nuovo: This 1913 reference piece on Marsico Nuovo and Potenza — the Lucanian diocese. Umberto Benigni gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the mountain flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Italian south. Its 11th-century see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mendez-and-gu: A 1913 entry on Mendez and Gualaquiza — the Ecuadorian vicariate. Andrew MacErlean gives its founding story. Its bishops guard the jungle flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A mission of the Amazon west. Its 1893 founding is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-gonzale: Cardinal Mendoza was the great cardinal of Spain who served the Catholic Monarchs. This entry traces his career, his power, and his patronage. The third king of Spain: his vast power nearly rivaled the Catholic Monarchs he so loyally served.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piacenza: Piacenza, the Emilian city of the Po plain, became a diocese rich in Romanesque art. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The Church in the city of the equestrian statues: its noble cathedral is a pure Romanesque gem.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siguenza: Sigüenza became the diocese of Castile's hill town. This entry covers its bishops, its cathedral, and its history. The faith of the Henares valley: its Gothic cathedral crowns the town in Castile's hills in the province of Guadalajara in Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-southern-vict: Southern Victoria Nyanza became the vicariate of the African lakes. This entry covers its missionaries, its stations, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the White Fathers: its mission stations dot the lake in the 1890s' decades in the vicariate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spinoza: Spinoza was the philosopher of the geometric Ethics. This long entry examines his substance, his God, and his influence. The lens-grinder of Amsterdam: his bold Ethics shook the 1600s in the Hague of the Dutch in the Republic of the provinces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-conrad-of-: St. Conrad of Piacenza was the hermit of Noto. This entry traces his hunt, his cave, and his cult. The penitent of the Sicilian hills: his lonely cave crowned Noto in the 1340s' Sicily in the south of the island.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanza: The stanza is the verse paragraph of poetry. This entry traces its Italian, its forms, and its use. The room of the poet's house: its measured verses crowned the canzone in the 1200s' courts in the halls of the lords.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-telesphorus-o: Telesphorus of Cosenza was the prophet of the age. This entry traces his Joachim, his visions, and his fame. The seer of the Calabrian hills: his wild visions crowned Cosenza in the 1300s' Sila in the hills of the Calabria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-of-g: Theodore of Gaza was the Greek humanist. This long entry examines his 1400s, his Aristotle, and his Rome. The scholar of the Renaissance court: his new Aristotle crowned Rome in the 1450s of the Bessarion in the very old curia.
doe-osti-3362797-seismic-elastic-double-: Faults got double-beam-characterized, and this DOE text selects CO2 storage sites. The pages detail the seismic findings. The geologists get their data. The selection was site. The data were geologist. The 2 were CO. The storage were site. The geologists were data.
doe-osti-3449289-sensitivity-analysis-an: Ceramic breeders got sensitivity-optimized, and this DOE project covers design optimization. The pages detail the analysis findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The report was project. The data were nuclear. The breeders were ceramic. The optimization were design.
nasa-tm-19650017698-prediction-of-propel:
J F Thompson and M E Nein, in Marshall's Propulsion and Vehicle Engineering Laboratory, issued this study on March 16, 1965. Rocket propellant tanks must be pressurized so fuel flows to the engines at the right rate. Too little pressure starves an engine. Too much adds weight and risk to the tank system.

Their method uses dimensional analysis to predict what pressure a tank will need. That approach finds the key factors that govern a problem, then links them in a compact rule. Designers could estimate needs early, before detailed tests. For large Saturn-era tanks, a sound early estimate saved both time and costly redesign.
podcast-dannyjones-osdtHmlLTzA:
Ben Van Kerkwyk returns to Danny Jones with what he calls new proof for computers in ancient Egypt. He studies fine stone work and says some of it shows machine-grade care. His word computer stands for lost high tech, not laptops of stone.

Van Kerkwyk points to flat faces, true cuts, and cores he says no hand tool could leave. He argues a lost culture had the tools and then fell from view. Jones asks what the tombs and texts say to back him. Listeners get the newest form of his case. The library files the talk as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-kWo6QNgr-zA:
Writer David Holthouse tells Rogan his story for episode 2129 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Holthouse is a journalist whose best-known work is painfully personal. As a boy he was assaulted. As a man he planned revenge on his attacker, then chose a different ending. His telling is chilling and human.

He walks Rogan through the years of rage, the plan he built, and the moment he stepped back from it. Rogan asks what the choice cost and gave him. The episode is true crime turned inward, a story of harm and restraint that stays with listeners long after it ends.
princess-maritza:
Percy Brebner wrote an adventure romance set at the invented court of Sturatzberg, where a princess moves among masked strangers, soldiers, and scheming nobles. Chapter titles promise a duel, an iron bracelet, a race for life, and a traitor unmasked before the close.

Figures such as Frina Mavrodin, Grigosie, and Baron Petrescu fill out the court intrigue, while early chapters follow truants, visitors, and a woman in a silk mask. Readers who enjoy old-style royal adventure get secret tokens, a castle in the hills, and loyalties tested at sword point.
the-day-of-days-an-extravaganza: Louis Joseph Vance calls The Day of Days an extravaganza. The Boston edition from Little, Brown, and Company is dated 1913 under copyrights of 1912 and 1913. Pictures are by Arthur William Brown, and a frontispiece is captioned with a line asking a lady to be the speaker's guest at the theatre that night. A list of Vance's other books heads the front matter: The Brass Bowl, The Black Bag, The Bandbox, The Destroying Angel, and Terence O'Rourke. Only the front matter is present here, so the tale itself does not appear.
the-old-roman-world-the-grandeur-and-fai: John Lord, LL.D., wrote The Old Roman World, on the grandeur and failure of Roman civilization. Only the contents are present here, in detailed chapter summaries, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The summaries show the plan of the book. One chapter covers Roman conquests from the kings through the civil wars. Another treats the material grandeur of the empire. A third describes the wonders of ancient Rome, its temples, aqueducts, forums, and baths. A closing chapter turns to Roman art.
thyrza: George Gissing's novel Thyrza is presented through a contents list of thirty-nine chapters. Early headings place scenes among hills, introduce an idealist, and settle into a corner of Lambeth. Thyrza sings, a golden prospect opens, and fortune tempts the characters. Later headings bring confession, the end of the dream, three letters, Thyrza waiting, and her return. Walnut Tree Walk and sea music recur as settings. A contents list alone is on these pages, so Gissing's novel itself does not appear here.
